Amazon Rainforest. The Amazon Rainforest is the world's largest tropical rainforest, spanning roughly 5.5 million square kilometers across nine countries with Brazil containing approximately 60% of its territory. Often called "the lungs of the Earth," it generates approximately 6–9% of the world's oxygen and regulates global climate patterns through its vast carbon stores and water cycling. Home to an estimated 10% of all species on Earth and to dozens of indigenous nations, the Amazon remains one of humanity's most biodiverse and ecologically significant ecosystems. First, covers an area roughly equivalent to the continental United States; divided among Brazil, Peru, Colombia, and six other nations. Additionally, named after the Amazon River, which flows through it and discharges more water than the next seven largest rivers combined. Equally important, contains an estimated 10% of all species known to science; roughly half are found nowhere else; thousands of species remain undocumented. Worth noting is home to indigenous peoples including the Yanomami, Kayapó, and dozens of other nations with continuous cultural presence spanning millennia. Another key fact: produces roughly 20% of the world's oxygen; absorbs roughly 2 billion tons of carbon dioxide annually, making it critical for climate regulation. Also, experiences "flying rivers"—water vapor released by trees forms rainfall that moves westward and sustains other ecosystems across South America. Less well known, facing rapid deforestation for cattle ranching, agriculture, and logging; deforestation rates have accelerated dramatically since the 1970s. The detail most often asked about: contains vast medicinal plant diversity; indigenous knowledge systems have identified thousands of pharmaceutical compounds; Western science has explored only a fraction.
